newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH APARTMENT PRICE RISE FLATTENING - SURVEY.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH APARTMENT PRICE RISE FLATTENING - SURVEY.

text.p: The rise in prices of apartments in Finland is flattening out, while prices of detached homes are still rising, according to an industry barometer published on Tuesday by Finnish real estate group PSW Kiinteistomaailma.
"The price rise that began last year seems to be slowing down," PSW said in its semi-annual survey.
Altogether 163 real estate agents from 33 towns took part in the spring survey, which assessed the outlook for the housing market over the next six months.
Now 42 percent of agents surveyed expected prices of small apartments to rise further, down from 71 percent last autumn.

In a research note dated May 9 and received on Tuesday, Protos Stockbrokers warned that low interest rates had boosted housing prices in the first quarter by more than 30 percent on the previous quarter and that the upward trend was likely to continue this year.
However, the pace of the increase was likely to slow down towards year-end, Protos said.
Protos warned of the possibility of overheating in the housing sector, and predicted that housing construction would increase 20 to 30 percent this year and next.
Housing prices were likely to continue to rise if Finland joined the planned third stage of European economic and monetary union from the beginning, Protos said.
It based this view on the assumption that Finnish interest rates would remain at the German level until the end of 1998.
That level of interest rates "seems to be clearly too low for the Finnish economy," Protos said.
"Low interest rates will keep economic growth very high and will probably feed the increase in housing prices," Protos said.
A recent government-commissioned report on economic and monetary union (EMU) had failed to take into account the risk of overheating on the housing market, it said.
"The Bank of Finland is unlikely to raise short-term interest rates because of EMU," Protos said.
The current long-end yield spread over German Bunds was justified considering the risk of a delay in Finland's EMU membership, it said.
